(2) Verification of conformational dynamics: FRET-based live-cell conformational reporter systems will be developed to monitor real-time conformational changes in 2B during infection. (3) Targeted intervention: Development of small-molecule inhibitors based on the stem-loop hinge region and interaction interfaces, followed by validation of their antiviral efficacy. (4) Pathogenic mechanisms: Elucidate how differences in the membrane environment of 2B in different tissues/cell types determine viral pathogenicity. (5) Cross-virus comparisons: Systematically compare the conformational dynamics and membrane environment responsiveness of 2B proteins from different picornavirus genera to test whether the “membrane stress sensor” concept has a broader applicability. This framework offers a mechanistic basis for anti-enterovirus drug design and may inform studies on other viroporins with similarly broad functional repertoires.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionThe genus Enterovirus within the family Picornaviridae comprises over 250 clinically significant serotypes that circulate worldwide [1–3]. Enterovirus infections manifest with a diverse spectrum of clinical presentations, including upper and lower respiratory tract illnesses, gastroenteritis, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, conjunctivitis, myocarditis, severe neonatal sepsis-like disease, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis (AFP), and AFM [3–6]. Important human pathogens within this genus include coxsackieviruses, enterovirus A71 (EVA71), enterovirus D68 (EVD68), echoviruses, and poliovirus (PV) [7–9]. Although these viruses share characteristics such as a small genome, rapid evolution, and broad pathogenic spectrum, targeted antiviral drugs remain absent. The functional pleiotropy of nonstructural protein 2B has emerged as a major obstacle to rational drug design. Understanding how a single ~100-amino-acid protein can engage in such disparate pathways is the central question addressed in this review.Enteroviruses possess a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome of approximately 7.5 kb in length [10–12]. A single open reading frame encodes a polyprotein that is proteolytically processed into three precursor regions: P1 (structural proteins VP1–VP4) and non-structural regions P2 and P3 [13]. The 2B protein, together with 2A (protease) [14,15] and 2C (helicase/ATPase) [16–18], constitutes the P2 region of the viral genome. Whereas 2A and 3C perform well-defined enzymatic functions, namely the proteolytic cleavage of viral and host targets [19,20], 2B is remarkable for its broad functional repertoire. Understanding how a single ~100-amino-acid protein can engage in such disparate pathways is the central question addressed in this review.The 2B protein is a non-structural protein of approximately 100 amino acids, encoded by the enterovirus genome [21,22]. Since its discovery in the 1980s, it has been defined as a “viroporin,” a protein that disrupts ion homeostasis by forming transmembrane hydrophilic pores [23–25]. Across viral families, viroporins share conserved strategies of membrane perturbation, including pore formation, lipid bilayer disordering, and membrane curvature sensing, underscoring the evolutionary convergence of these mechanisms [26,27]. Well-characterized examples include HCV p7, influenza A M2, and Human Immunodeficiency Virus type 1 (HIV-1) Vpu, each of which exploits distinct membrane-targeting mechanisms while sharing a common capacity to dysregulate host ion homeostasis [28–31]. The enterovirus 2B protein extends this paradigm with a uniquely dynamic topology that may enable membrane stress sensing. This framework, which has dominated research for three decades, successfully explains the effects of 2B on calcium signaling and membrane permeability during early viral replication. However, intensive research over the past decade has revealed a functional breadth that far exceeds the scope of traditional pore models. Limitations of the viroporin model and the membrane stress sensor hypothesisFirst, the pore model cannot explain the breadth of protein–protein interactions (PPI) in cell membranes. 2B has been shown to directly interacts with multiple host proteins, including Bax [32], NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) [33], Karyopherin subunit alpha 1 (KPNA1) [34], Interleukin enhancer-binding factor 2 (ILF2) [35], Cluster of Differentiation 74 (CD74) [36], Voltage-Dependent Anion Channel 3 (VDAC3) [37], and N-Acetyltransferase 8 (NAT8) [38]. These interactions span apoptosis, inflammation, nuclear transport, and immune recognition, extending far beyond the scope of ion-channel activity.Second, the pore model cannot explain species-specific functional divergence. The stable association of EVD68 2B with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane depends on an acidic environment; when autophagic flux is blocked and vesicle acidification is insufficient, 2B cannot be stably anchored to the membrane [39], a phenomenon not observed for coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) or PV. The E40K mutation in CVB3 2B produces a quasi-infectious phenotype that can be rescued by trans-complementation [40], suggesting differences in the functional plasticity among enterovirus 2B proteins. Moreover, the subcellular localization differs: CVB3 2B is primarily localized to the Golgi apparatus, whereas PV 2B exhibits a distinct topological orientation [22,41].Third, the pore model cannot accommodate discrepancies between functional redundancy and pore essentiality. The impact of 2B deletion on viral replication varies considerably among viruses: siRNA-mediated knockdown of EVA71 2B markedly reduces but does not abolish viral replication [42], while a CVB3 2B-derived peptide potently inhibits the virus without achieving sterilizing clearance [43].Fourth, the pore model cannot incorporate post-transcriptional RNA-level regulation, such as N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification of Lon Peptidase 1 (LONP1) mRNA. A direct RNA-modification link between 2B and ferroptosis was established in a recent study [44].In summary, the existing framework can no longer accommodate the functional breadth and depth of 2B. Studies have shown that the transmembrane helices of 2B can respond with conformational sensitivity to physicochemical parameters, such as membrane lipid composition and pH, with distinct conformational states corresponding to different downstream effector outputs, a characteristic that endows 2B with “sensor” functionality. Therefore, this study proposes a new theoretical framework: defining 2B as a membrane stress sensor, whose diverse functional outputs arise from its conformational responsiveness to changes in the membrane microenvironment. This framework comprises three operational criteria.We emphasize that this framework is a testable working hypothesis and not a validated mechanism. Direct experimental evidence for conformational switching under different membrane conditions is currently lacking, and the three operational criteria defined below remain to be experimentally verified.Conformational responsiveness to changes in the membrane microenvironmentThe transmembrane helices (H1/H2) and stem-loop hinge region of 2B adopt different conformational states in different membrane environments. These environmental parameters include lipid composition, membrane curvature, and pH values. These conformational states can be captured using structural biology approaches [e.g. such as fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR)].Distinct conformational states correspond to different functional outputsSpecific conformational states can expose different protein interaction interfaces, thereby selectively activating pathways such as calcium signaling, apoptosis, pyroptosis, and immune evasion. Conformation-locking mutants exhibit directional changes in their functional spectra.Membrane microenvironment is essential for functional switchingThe functional switching of 2B strictly depends on changes in the membrane environmental parameters. For example, differences in lipid composition among the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondrial, and autophagosomal membranes may directly determine whether 2B activates Bax or NLRP3, and disruption of the pH gradient can lead to 2B degradation or its inactivation.Throughout this review, we distinguished three categories of evidence: (i) experimentally validated: conclusions directly supported by published experimental data, including mutagenesis, co-immunoprecipitation, FRET, and functional assays. (ii) Inferred from indirect evidence: conclusions consistent with the available data but not yet confirmed by direct experimentation. (iii) Speculative: components of the membrane stress sensor hypothesis that generate testable predictions but currently lack experimental support. title_original: Enterovirus 2B protein: From viroporin to membrane stress sensor, mechanistic principles of multi-pathway regulation

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to address the functional pleiotropy of nonstructural protein 2B, which has hindered rational drug design for human enteroviruses. The traditional viroporin model, which limits 2B to ion channel formation, fails to explain its interactions with host factors and functional divergence among enteroviruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a theoretical and computational analysis of the enterovirus 2B protein, focusing on its role in human enteroviruses. It examines the protein's interactions with host factors and its functional divergence across different serotypes, including EV-A71, EV-D68, CV-A6, and CV-A16.
analysis.methods: The study employs computational modeling and structural analysis to propose a framework in which the 2B protein functions as a membrane stress sensor. It explores conformational dynamics, lipid composition, pH changes, and their impact on calcium signaling, cell death pathways, and immune evasion.
analysis.main_results: The study reports that the transmembrane helices of 2B sense changes in the membrane microenvironment, including lipid composition, pH, and curvature. It also highlights the protein's direct interactions with host factors such as Bax, NLRP3, and KPNA1, and its role in coordinating calcium signaling, cell death pathway selection, and immune evasion.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret their findings as supporting a novel hypothesis that the 2B protein acts as a membrane stress sensor, which provides a unified explanation for its diverse functions. This framework introduces a new perspective on 2B's role, moving beyond the traditional viroporin model.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The framework offers a mechanistic foundation for understanding 2B's role in enterovirus pathogenesis, which can guide the development of rational anti-enteroviral drugs. It also highlights key evidence gaps that need to be addressed for further research.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges key uncertainties, such as whether 2B exhibits calcium ion selectivity or forms a nonselective pore, and whether the pH dependence of EVD68 2B is mediated by a specific histidine residue. These limitations suggest that the evidence is moderate, requiring further experimental validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study proposes a novel framework in which the enterovirus 2B protein functions as a membrane stress sensor, overcoming the limitations of the traditional viroporin model. The research highlights the protein's ability to sense changes in the membrane microenvironment, including lipid composition, pH, and curvature, and coordinate calcium signaling, cell death pathway selection, and immune evasion. The findings suggest that 2B interacts with host factors such as Bax, NLRP3, and KPNA1, and its functional divergence among different enteroviruses may be explained by this new model. The study identifies key uncertainties, such as calcium ion selectivity and pH dependence, which require further experimental validation. The framework provides a mechanistic basis for understanding 2B's role in enterovirus pathogenesis and may inform future drug design efforts. However, the evidence is moderate due to the need for additional studies to confirm the proposed mechanisms.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决非结构蛋白 2B 的功能多效性,该多效性阻碍了 人肠道病毒 的合理药物设计。传统的病毒孔蛋白模型将 2B 限制为离子通道的形成,无法解释其与 宿主 因子的相互作用以及肠道病毒之间的功能差异。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对肠道病毒 2B 蛋白的理论和计算分析,重点关注其在 人肠道病毒 中的作用。它检查了该蛋白质与 宿主 因子的相互作用及其在不同血清型(包括 EV-A71、EV-D68、CV-A6 和 CV-A16)之间的功能差异。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究采用计算模型和结构分析提出了一个框架,其中 2B 蛋白充当膜应力传感器。它探讨了构象动力学、脂质组成、pH 变化及其对钙信号传导、细胞死亡途径和免疫逃避的影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 研究报告称,2B 的跨膜螺旋可以感知膜微环境的变化,包括脂质成分、pH 值和曲率。它还强调了该蛋白与 Bax、NLRP3 和 KPNA1 等 宿主 因子的直接相互作用,及其在协调钙信号传导、细胞死亡途径选择和免疫逃避中的作用。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将他们的发现解释为支持一个新的假设,即 2B 蛋白充当膜应激传感器,这为其不同的功能提供了统一的解释。该框架超越了传统的病毒孔蛋白模型,引入了关于 2B 作用的新视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该框架为理解2B在肠道病毒发病机制中的作用提供了机制基础,可以指导合理的抗肠道病毒药物的开发。它还强调了进一步研究需要解决的关键证据差距。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究承认了一些关键的不确定性,例如 2B 是否表现出钙离子选择性或形成非选择性孔,以及 EVD68 2B 的 pH 依赖性是否由特定组氨酸残基介导。这些局限性表明证据是中等的,需要进一步的实验验证。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决非结构蛋白 2B 的功能多效性,该多效性阻碍了 人肠道病毒 的合理药物设计。传统的病毒孔蛋白模型将 2B 限制为离子通道的形成,无法解释其与 宿主 因子的相互作用以及肠道病毒之间的功能差异。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是对肠道病毒 2B 蛋白的理论和计算分析,重点关注其在 人肠道病毒 中的作用。它检查了该蛋白质与 宿主 因子的相互作用及其在不同血清型(包括 EV-A71、EV-D68、CV-A6 和 CV-A16)之间的功能差异。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究采用计算模型和结构分析提出了一个框架,其中 2B 蛋白充当膜应力传感器。它探讨了构象动力学、脂质组成、pH 变化及其对钙信号传导、细胞死亡途径和免疫逃避的影响。
analysis_zh.main_results: 研究报告称,2B 的跨膜螺旋可以感知膜微环境的变化,包括脂质成分、pH 值和曲率。它还强调了该蛋白与 Bax、NLRP3 和 KPNA1 等 宿主 因子的直接相互作用,及其在协调钙信号传导、细胞死亡途径选择和免疫逃避中的作用。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将他们的发现解释为支持一个新的假设,即 2B 蛋白充当膜应激传感器,这为其不同的功能提供了统一的解释。该框架超越了传统的病毒孔蛋白模型,引入了关于 2B 作用的新视角。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该框架为理解2B在肠道病毒发病机制中的作用提供了机制基础,可以指导合理的抗肠道病毒药物的开发。它还强调了进一步研究需要解决的关键证据差距。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究承认了一些关键的不确定性,例如 2B 是否表现出钙离子选择性或形成非选择性孔,以及 EVD68 2B 的 pH 依赖性是否由特定组氨酸残基介导。这些局限性表明证据是中等的,需要进一步的实验验证。

title: Epidemiology and lagged climatic drivers of pediatric viral lower respiratory tract infections in Tianjin, China (2023–2025)

source_records.title: Epidemiology and lagged climatic drivers of pediatric viral lower respiratory tract infections in Tianjin, China (2023–2025)

full_text: BackgroundFollowing the lifting of pandemic-era restrictions, China experienced a sharp resurgence in pediatric respiratory infections; however, post-pandemic epidemiological and climatic data on lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from the temperate continental climate of northern China remain scarce.MethodsIn this retrospective, single-center surveillance study, we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of six respiratory viruses in children hospitalized with LRTI in Tianjin and assessed their pathogen-specific, lagged climatic associations. Children aged 0–18 years hospitalized between January 2023 and December 2025 were tested by targeted next-generation sequencing for human rhinovirus (HRV), adenovirus (ADV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human bocavirus (HBoV), influenza virus (IFV), and human metapneumovirus (HMPV). Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%), and HMPV (4.0%). Age distributions differed by pathogen (p<0.05): RSV and HBoV predominated in infants and toddlers, HRV and HMPV in preschoolers, ADV in school-aged children, and IFV across the older preschool-to-school-age range; males predominated for all viruses except IFV. Five viruses peaked in December, whereas HBoV peaked uniquely in July. After adjustment for seasonality and secular trend, the unadjusted associations of IFV with humidity and temperature disappeared, indicating that they largely reflected shared seasonality. In contrast, RSV retained associations with temperature (RR 3.87, 95% CI 1.39–10.76) and wind speed (RR 5.46, 95% CI 2.39–12.47) at a 1-month lag, and HMPV with temperature (RR 13.3, 95% CI 1.64–108.3; imprecise given its low case count); HRV, ADV, and HBoV showed no independent climatic associations. Co-infections occurred in 116 cases (4.5%), most frequently HBoV+HRV (23.3%).ConclusionPost-pandemic pediatric viral LRTI in Tianjin shows distinctive pathogen-specific profiles in age, seasonality, and climatic sensitivity. The summer peak of HBoV and the seasonally independent climatic drivers of RSV and HMPV provide a preliminary basis that, if confirmed with higher-resolution data, could inform pathogen-tailored, climate-informed surveillance in northern Chinese megacities. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting and populationWe conducted a retrospective single-center surveillance study at the Department of Respiratory Medicine, Tianjin Children’s Hospital (Ma-Chang campus), the only tertiary-A comprehensive children’s hospital in Tianjin. The hospital is the principal pediatric referral center for Tianjin municipality and, for selected specialties, draws patients from across the wider North China Plain; publicly reported hospital-wide figures indicate roughly 17,000–20,000 pediatric admissions per year across all departments. Our cohort of 2,597 virologically confirmed viral LRTI cases represents the subset of hospitalized LRTI cases that were both tested and found positive for one of the six target viruses, not the total burden of pediatric LRTI hospitalization in Tianjin. A precise, denominator-based estimate of the proportion of all Tianjin pediatric LRTI hospitalizations captured by this cohort is not available, because no citywide pediatric LRTI hospitalization registry exists for comparison. As a tertiary referral center, the cohort is likely enriched for more severe disease and for cases referred from primary and secondary facilities; this referral pattern, and the resulting limit on generalizability to primary care, is revisited in the Discussion (Section 4.6).Eligible participants were children aged 0–18 years hospitalized with a clinical diagnosis of LRTI between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2025, from whom a respiratory specimen was submitted for routine viral testing. LRTI was defined clinically, following the 2019 Chinese Pediatric Society guideline for community-acquired pneumonia (Subspecialty Group of Respiratory Diseases, 2019), as cough or fever (axillary temperature ≥38 °C) together with at least one of: tachypnoea, wheezing, crackles on auscultation, or imaging evidence of pneumonia or bronchiolitis. This definition captures the clinical syndromes of pneumonia and bronchiolitis and excludes isolated upper respiratory tract infection. We excluded children with pre-existing chronic respiratory disease, congenital airway malformations, documented immunodeficiency, active malignancy, or concurrent infection by pathogens outside the predefined six-virus panel. This last criterion operated at the level of the child rather than of the laboratory result: whenever the tNGS report carried a Class A detection of a bacterial, atypical or non-panel viral pathogen alongside one of the six target viruses, the case was removed from the cohort at eligibility screening, so no such child contributes to any analysis reported here. For viruses prone to subclinical carriage, chiefly HRV and HBoV, a detection was considered clinically causative only when the tNGS reporting algorithm assigned a pathogenicity Class A grade, the clinical picture matched the corresponding viral syndrome, and other plausible infectious causes had been clinically excluded (residual misclassification risk for these two viruses is discussed in Section 4.6). For descriptive analyses, children were stratified a priori into four age categories: infants (<1 year), toddlers (1–2 years), preschoolers (3–5 years) and school-aged children (≥6 years). All records were de-identified before analysis. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Tianjin Children’s Hospital (approval number 2024-LXKY-023); written informed consent was waived given the retrospective design and full de-identification of the dataset.2.2Pathogen detectionRespiratory specimens (sputum, the predominant type; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, BALF; nasopharyngeal swabs; and oropharyngeal swabs) were collected following standardized clinical protocols, placed into viral transport medium, and transported within two hours at 2–8 °C to the clinical laboratory. Total nucleic acids were extracted on an automated platform following the manufacturer’s instructions. All specimens were tested with the same commercial targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) panel, which simultaneously screens for respiratory bacteria, viruses, atypical pathogens and antimicrobial-resistance markers. Library construction, ultra-multiplex amplification of pathogen-specific genomic regions and Illumina-compatible high-throughput sequencing were performed following the manufacturer’s recommended workflow, with reads aligned against a curated pathogen reference database (Li et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025). The vendor’s reporting algorithm assigned each detected organism a clinical pathogenicity grade, from Class A (highest confidence) through lower-confidence grades. The panel was introduced during 2023 and reached full clinical implementation in the fourth quarter of that year, after which testing volume remained broadly stable through 2024 and 2025. Monthly counts of tNGS requests could not be retrieved from the laboratory information system for the whole study window, so this account of testing volume rests on the laboratory’s implementation record rather than on an auditable series of test counts, and it should be read as such.The grade is a composite call rather than a single read-count cut-off. It is generated by an integrated scoring system that combines normalized read counts (reads per million, RPM), the breadth of genome coverage achieved across the targeted regions, and species-level annotation of pathogenicity against a curated reference database; Class A is assigned to organisms that meet the pre-specified RPM and coverage criteria for a clinically significant pathogen. The numerical RPM and coverage cut-offs behind the grade are proprietary to the assay vendor and are not released to the ordering laboratory; we are therefore unable to report them, and the grade as issued was the only form in which this information was available to us. Grading was prospective in the sense that it was performed by the clinical laboratory at the time the routine diagnostic report was issued and used for patient care, and the research team did not re-adjudicate the classifications retrospectively. No Class A detection was subsequently excluded on the grounds of clinical mismatch, because the Class A flag served as an inclusion criterion for the six-virus panel rather than as the sole determinant of clinical causality; for HRV and HBoV, the additional clinical adjudication described in Section 2.1 was applied instead.The full panel detects a broader range of organisms than the six viruses analyzed here. Common bacterial pathogens reported by the full panel include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis and Staphylococcus aureus; the atypical pathogens include Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae; and respiratory viruses outside the six-virus panel, including parainfluenza viruses, seasonal coronaviruses and SARS-CoV-2, are likewise covered. Consistent with the eligibility criteria set out in Section 2.1, a child in whom any of these organisms was reported concurrently with one of the six target viruses was excluded from the cohort at screening rather than merely omitted from the analysis; the cases analysed here are therefore restricted to children whose Class A detections fell entirely within the six-virus panel. We restricted the present analysis to the six respiratory viruses (HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV, IFV, covering both influenza A and B, and HMPV) flagged at the highest pathogenicity grade (Class A), for three reasons. First, these six viruses are the pathogens for which pathogen-specific climatic drivers are most biologically plausible and best characterized, allowing direct comparison with prior lagged-climate studies (Baker et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2021). Second, restricting to Class A calls minimizes the inclusion of low-confidence or incidental detections. Third, bacterial and atypical pathogens are subject to different detection biases (for example, antibiotic pretreatment and colonization) and different climate–transmission mechanisms, and were therefore outside the scope of this analysis. Co-infections, defined as concurrent Class A detection of two or more of the six target viruses in the same specimen, were identified and are described in Section 2.4.2.3Meteorological dataMonthly city-wide meteorological summaries for Tianjin from January 2023 to December 2025 (n = 36 months) were obtained from the Tianjin Meteorological Bureau and comprised mean atmospheric pressure (hPa), mean wind speed (m/s), mean air temperature (°C), mean relative humidity (%), precipitation (mm) and mean daily sunshine duration (hours). Routine quality assurance included unit verification and column-order auditing across reporting periods. The meteorological series was time-aligned with the monthly aggregated viral case counts before analysis.We used monthly rather than daily or weekly data because the records available from the Tianjin Meteorological Bureau for this study period were supplied at monthly resolution; daily or weekly city-wide summaries were not accessible for the full 2023–2025 window. Finer (for example, weekly) resolution would allow more precise estimation of short-lag effects and is standard in DLNM-based climate–infection studies (Gasparrini et al., 2010; Li et al., 2025); we discuss this resolution constraint further in Section 4.6.2.4Statistical analysisCategorical data are presented as counts (percentages) and compared between groups with Pearson’s χ2 test; the assumption of an equal sex ratio was tested with the exact binomial test, and inter-pathogen age differences with the Kruskal–Wallis test. Daily case records were aggregated to monthly totals and merged with the meteorological time series. Yates’ continuity correction was applied to 2 × 2 comparisons.Co-infections were tabulated separately from the mono-infection pathogen spectrum. The primary pathogen-spectrum analysis (case counts, proportions, and demographic and specimen-type distributions in Section 3.1) attributes each specimen to a single, mutually exclusive pathogen row, so the per-pathogen counts in Table 1 sum to the total of 2,597 virus-positive cases; co-infection structure itself (pairwise combinations, and multiplicity) is tabulated separately, with each co-infected specimen contributing to every virus it carried, and is described in Section 3.4.Table 1Demographic and specimen characteristics of pediatric viral LRTI cases by pathogen.PathogenN (% of all positive)Male, n (%)Female, n (%)Sex p-valueAge, median (IQR), yLower respiratory tract specimen, n (%)HRV796 (30.7)471 (59.2)325 (40.8)<0.0014.0 (2.0–6.0)660 (82.9)ADV692 (26.6)425 (61.4)267 (38.6)<0.0016.0 (3.0–8.0)485 (70.1)RSV536 (20.6)304 (56.7)232 (43.3)0.0023.0 (1.0–4.0)454 (84.7)HBoV313 (12.1)179 (57.2)134 (42.8)0.0132.0 (1.0–4.0)277 (88.5)IFV155 (6.0)83 (53.5)72 (46.5)0.425.0 (2.0–7.0)123 (79.4)HMPV105 (4.0)66 (62.9)39 (37.1)0.0114.0 (1.8–6.0)74 (70.5)Pathogen counts are mutually exclusive per specimen (see Section 2.4), so the column totals sum to 2,597. Co-infected specimens, in which two or more Class A viruses were detected concurrently, are tabulated separately in Section 3.4, where each such specimen contributes to the count of every virus it carried; those pairwise counts are not reflected in the totals above. Sex p-values are from the exact binomial test against a 50:50 null; age is median (IQR) in years; Lower respiratory tract specimen = sputum or BALF.Pathogen–climate co-variation was screened with Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ) on the full monthly series and re-examined within meteorological seasons (spring, March–May; summer, June–August; autumn, September–November; winter, December–February).Lagged meteorological effects were examined in two complementary ways. First, cross-correlation functions were computed over lags of 0–6 months for temperature, relative humidity and wind speed. Second, lag-specific relative risks (RR) were derived from quasi-Poisson GLMs with a log link (Bhaskaran et al., 2013; Gasparrini, 2011; Imai et al., 2015) of the form log(μt) = α + β × Xt−L, where μt is the expected monthly case count in month t and Xt−L the meteorological exposure shifted back by L months (L = 0, 1, ..., 6). Because this analysis spans 126 model fits (6 pathogens × 3 variables × 7 lags), no formal correction for multiple comparisons was applied; signals reaching p<0.01 (for example, RSV with wind speed at a 1-month lag) are interpreted as relatively robust, whereas signals in the 0.01 to 0.05 range (for example, HMPV with temperature, and RSV with temperature) are flagged as exploratory. RR values are reported per clinically interpretable unit (5 °C for temperature, 10% for relative humidity and 0.5 m/s for wind speed), each chosen to approximate the interquartile span of the corresponding variable. Standard errors were corrected for overdispersion (Pearson dispersion parameter φ ≥ 1). For every pathogen × exposure combination, the lag at which the absolute log-RR was largest among significant lags is reported as the peak RR; the resulting post-hoc selection across candidate lags is discussed as a source of potential effect-size inflation in Section 4.6.This graded reading is a descriptive convention and does not control the family-wise error rate. Under the null hypothesis, roughly six of the 126 fits would be expected to reach p<0.05 by chance, and a Bonferroni-corrected threshold would fall at p<0.0004. We report uncorrected p-values on the reasoning that the six pathogens address distinct epidemiological questions rather than a single universal null, an approach with precedent in exploratory analyses of this kind (Rothman, 1990); the accompanying Type I error risk is set out explicitly in Section 4.6. Two associations in the 0.01 to 0.05 range are nonetheless carried into the Discussion, RSV with temperature and HMPV with temperature, and both are presented there as provisional, the HMPV signal explicitly as hypothesis-generating; no clinical or public health recommendation in this paper rests on either of them alone.Because the peak RR is the largest of up to seven correlated estimates, it is biased away from the null and its confidence interval is narrower than the selection process warrants, a general property of effect estimates identified by crossing a significance threshold in underpowered analyses (Ioannidis, 2008). Co-infections occurred in 116 cases (4.5%), most frequently HBoV+HRV (23.3%).ConclusionPost-pandemic pediatric viral LRTI in Tianjin shows distinctive pathogen-specific profiles in age, seasonality, and climatic sensitivity. The summer peak of HBoV and the seasonally independent climatic drivers of RSV and HMPV provide a preliminary basis that, if confirmed with higher-resolution data, could inform pathogen-tailored, climate-informed surveillance in northern Chinese megacities.
full_text_sections.methods: 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting and populationWe conducted a retrospective single-center surveillance study at the Department of Respiratory Medicine, Tianjin Children’s Hospital (Ma-Chang campus), the only tertiary-A comprehensive children’s hospital in Tianjin. The hospital is the principal pediatric referral center for Tianjin municipality and, for selected specialties, draws patients from across the wider North China Plain; publicly reported hospital-wide figures indicate roughly 17,000–20,000 pediatric admissions per year across all departments. Our cohort of 2,597 virologically confirmed viral LRTI cases represents the subset of hospitalized LRTI cases that were both tested and found positive for one of the six target viruses, not the total burden of pediatric LRTI hospitalization in Tianjin. A precise, denominator-based estimate of the proportion of all Tianjin pediatric LRTI hospitalizations captured by this cohort is not available, because no citywide pediatric LRTI hospitalization registry exists for comparison. As a tertiary referral center, the cohort is likely enriched for more severe disease and for cases referred from primary and secondary facilities; this referral pattern, and the resulting limit on generalizability to primary care, is revisited in the Discussion (Section 4.6).Eligible participants were children aged 0–18 years hospitalized with a clinical diagnosis of LRTI between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2025, from whom a respiratory specimen was submitted for routine viral testing. LRTI was defined clinically, following the 2019 Chinese Pediatric Society guideline for community-acquired pneumonia (Subspecialty Group of Respiratory Diseases, 2019), as cough or fever (axillary temperature ≥38 °C) together with at least one of: tachypnoea, wheezing, crackles on auscultation, or imaging evidence of pneumonia or bronchiolitis. This definition captures the clinical syndromes of pneumonia and bronchiolitis and excludes isolated upper respiratory tract infection. We excluded children with pre-existing chronic respiratory disease, congenital airway malformations, documented immunodeficiency, active malignancy, or concurrent infection by pathogens outside the predefined six-virus panel. This last criterion operated at the level of the child rather than of the laboratory result: whenever the tNGS report carried a Class A detection of a bacterial, atypical or non-panel viral pathogen alongside one of the six target viruses, the case was removed from the cohort at eligibility screening, so no such child contributes to any analysis reported here. For viruses prone to subclinical carriage, chiefly HRV and HBoV, a detection was considered clinically causative only when the tNGS reporting algorithm assigned a pathogenicity Class A grade, the clinical picture matched the corresponding viral syndrome, and other plausible infectious causes had been clinically excluded (residual misclassification risk for these two viruses is discussed in Section 4.6). For descriptive analyses, children were stratified a priori into four age categories: infants (<1 year), toddlers (1–2 years), preschoolers (3–5 years) and school-aged children (≥6 years). All records were de-identified before analysis. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Tianjin Children’s Hospital (approval number 2024-LXKY-023); written informed consent was waived given the retrospective design and full de-identification of the dataset.2.2Pathogen detectionRespiratory specimens (sputum, the predominant type; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, BALF; nasopharyngeal swabs; and oropharyngeal swabs) were collected following standardized clinical protocols, placed into viral transport medium, and transported within two hours at 2–8 °C to the clinical laboratory. Total nucleic acids were extracted on an automated platform following the manufacturer’s instructions. All specimens were tested with the same commercial targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) panel, which simultaneously screens for respiratory bacteria, viruses, atypical pathogens and antimicrobial-resistance markers. Library construction, ultra-multiplex amplification of pathogen-specific genomic regions and Illumina-compatible high-throughput sequencing were performed following the manufacturer’s recommended workflow, with reads aligned against a curated pathogen reference database (Li et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025). The vendor’s reporting algorithm assigned each detected organism a clinical pathogenicity grade, from Class A (highest confidence) through lower-confidence grades. The panel was introduced during 2023 and reached full clinical implementation in the fourth quarter of that year, after which testing volume remained broadly stable through 2024 and 2025. Monthly counts of tNGS requests could not be retrieved from the laboratory information system for the whole study window, so this account of testing volume rests on the laboratory’s implementation record rather than on an auditable series of test counts, and it should be read as such.The grade is a composite call rather than a single read-count cut-off. It is generated by an integrated scoring system that combines normalized read counts (reads per million, RPM), the breadth of genome coverage achieved across the targeted regions, and species-level annotation of pathogenicity against a curated reference database; Class A is assigned to organisms that meet the pre-specified RPM and coverage criteria for a clinically significant pathogen. The numerical RPM and coverage cut-offs behind the grade are proprietary to the assay vendor and are not released to the ordering laboratory; we are therefore unable to report them, and the grade as issued was the only form in which this information was available to us. Grading was prospective in the sense that it was performed by the clinical laboratory at the time the routine diagnostic report was issued and used for patient care, and the research team did not re-adjudicate the classifications retrospectively. No Class A detection was subsequently excluded on the grounds of clinical mismatch, because the Class A flag served as an inclusion criterion for the six-virus panel rather than as the sole determinant of clinical causality; for HRV and HBoV, the additional clinical adjudication described in Section 2.1 was applied instead.The full panel detects a broader range of organisms than the six viruses analyzed here. Common bacterial pathogens reported by the full panel include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis and Staphylococcus aureus; the atypical pathogens include Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae; and respiratory viruses outside the six-virus panel, including parainfluenza viruses, seasonal coronaviruses and SARS-CoV-2, are likewise covered. Consistent with the eligibility criteria set out in Section 2.1, a child in whom any of these organisms was reported concurrently with one of the six target viruses was excluded from the cohort at screening rather than merely omitted from the analysis; the cases analysed here are therefore restricted to children whose Class A detections fell entirely within the six-virus panel. We restricted the present analysis to the six respiratory viruses (HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV, IFV, covering both influenza A and B, and HMPV) flagged at the highest pathogenicity grade (Class A), for three reasons. First, these six viruses are the pathogens for which pathogen-specific climatic drivers are most biologically plausible and best characterized, allowing direct comparison with prior lagged-climate studies (Baker et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2021). Second, restricting to Class A calls minimizes the inclusion of low-confidence or incidental detections. full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Overall pathogen distribution and demographicsAcross 36 surveillance months we identified 2,597 virologically confirmed pediatric LRTI cases. HRV was the most frequently detected virus (796 cases, 30.7%), followed by ADV (692, 26.6%), RSV (536, 20.6%), HBoV (313, 12.1%), IFV (155, 6.0%) and HMPV (105, 4.0%) (Figure 2A; Table 1). Sputum was the predominant specimen type for HRV, RSV, HBoV, HMPV and IFV. The proportion of cases sampled from the lower airway (sputum or BALF) likewise differed across pathogens (χ2 = 73.7, df = 5, p < 0.001), ranging from 70.1% for ADV and 70.5% for HMPV to 88.5% for HBoV (Table 1). ADV was more evenly distributed across specimen types, with BALF (35.4%) and sputum (34.7%) contributing similar shares and nasopharyngeal swabs a further 29.6%, giving ADV a markedly higher BALF share than the other five viruses (Figure 2B). Annual case counts rose from 188 in 2023 to 1,027 in 2024 and 1,382 in 2025 (Figure 2C). The 2023 figures warrant particular caution on this account. The assay reached full clinical implementation only in the fourth quarter of that year (Section 2.2), so the 188 cases recorded in 2023 almost certainly under-represent circulation during the early post-pandemic period relative to 2024 and 2025, when testing volume was broadly stable. Subsequent analyses therefore emphasize pathogen composition, age distribution and seasonal timing, which are far less sensitive to testing volume than absolute case counts.Figure 2Overall pathogen spectrum and specimen characteristics of pediatric viral LRTI in Tianjin, 2023–2025. (A) Case distribution across the six viral pathogens, ranked by prevalence. (B) Specimen-type composition by pathogen. (C) Annual case burden, stacked by pathogen.Grouped bar and stacked bar chart panel showing (A) case numbers and percentages for six pathogens, (B) specimen composition by pathogen, and (C) annual case burden from 2023 to 2025. HRV and ADV have the highest positive cases, sputum is the most common specimen, and total case burden increases each year, with pathogen contribution shown by color.Two features of the assay bound the influence of testing volume without removing it. All six viruses sit on a single multiplex panel and are screened simultaneously in every specimen, so no virus could be tested more often than another, and a change in ordering volume alters which children were tested rather than which viruses were sought. What this cannot exclude is a shift in case mix: if tNGS was ordered preferentially for more severely ill children, and if the pathogen spectrum of severe admissions differs from that of milder ones, composition will move with ordering practice. The markedly higher BALF share of ADV (Figure 2B) is consistent with such a gradient, and the point is developed in Section 4.6.Boys predominated for HRV (59.2%, p<0.001), ADV (61.4%, p<0.001), RSV (56.7%, p=0.002), HBoV (57.2%, p=0.013) and HMPV (62.9%, p=0.011), whereas IFV showed a balanced sex ratio (53.5% male, p=0.42) (Table 1; Figure 3A). Although IFV was the only virus without a male excess, a χ2 test for heterogeneity across the six pathogens did not reach significance (χ2 = 5.77, df = 5, p = 0.33), and neither did the comparison of IFV against the other five viruses combined (χ2 = 1.68, df = 1, p = 0.20). The balanced ratio for IFV is therefore better read as a failure to demonstrate a male excess in the smallest of the larger groups (n = 155) than as evidence of a genuinely different sex distribution.Figure 3Demographic composition of pediatric viral LRTI by pathogen. (A) Sex distribution, with binomial-test significance markers. (B) Age (years) by pathogen (median, IQR), with jittered individual data points overlaid. Significance markers: *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001; ns = not significant.Bar chart on the left shows male and female sex distribution for six pathogens with males consistently higher for HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV, and HMPV; differences denoted by statistical significance symbols. Boxplot on the right displays age distribution in years for each pathogen with medians, interquartile ranges, and data points, indicating variation in median ages by pathogen.Age distributions differed sharply across pathogens (Kruskal–Wallis H = 372.7, p < 0.001; Figure 3B). Infants and toddlers carried most HBoV (median 2.0 [IQR 1.0–4.0] years) and RSV (3.0 [1.0–4.0]) cases; preschoolers were the main group for HRV (4.0 [2.0–6.0]) and HMPV (4.0 [1.8–6.0]); ADV predominated in school-aged children (6.0 [3.0–8.0]), while IFV spanned the older preschool-to-school-age range (median 5.0 [2.0–7.0]) (Table 1; Figure 3B).3.2Temporal distributionMonthly time-series of the six pathogens (Figure 4A) showed strong but pathogen-specific seasonality. HRV, ADV, RSV, IFV and HMPV all reached their annual maxima in December, consistent with the cold, dry continental winter being the dominant transmission season in northern China. The December peak of late 2024 (about 400 positive cases that month) was the largest monthly count of the surveillance period, with a smaller but still notable winter peak in December 2025. HBoV behaved differently, showing a single summer maximum in July. ADV showed a secondary peak in late spring (April–May), and HRV and ADV together produced the broadest seasonal envelope (March–December) of any pathogen. The seasonal heatmap (Figure 4B) summarizes these patterns: each virus shows at least one clearly defined month-of-year peak, and HBoV is the only virus to peak in a warm-season month (July). Because the heatmap is normalized row-wise, color intensity for each pathogen is scaled to its own monthly range; the visual prominence of a peak for a low-incidence pathogen (for example, HMPV) therefore does not indicate the same absolute case count as for a high-incidence pathogen (for example, HRV).Figure 4Temporal distribution of pediatric viral LRTI, 2023–2025. (A) Stacked monthly case counts by pathogen. The chart (panel A) shows case counts for HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV, IFV, and HMPV, with peaks observed between late 2024 and early 2025. The heatmap (panel B) presents mean cases per month for each virus, highlighting increased relative intensity for most pathogens in November and December, with values labeled within cells and a scale indicating intensity from low (yellow) to high (red).3.3Seasonal and meteorological analyses3.3.1Overall pathogen–climate correlationsOverall Spearman rank correlations (Figure 5A; Table 2) showed a significant positive correlation between HBoV and temperature (ρ = +0.34, p = 0.04). ADV (ρ = +0.32, p = 0.06), HRV (ρ = +0.28, p = 0.10) and RSV (ρ = +0.24, p = 0.16) showed positive but non-significant trends. IFV and HMPV showed non-significant negative correlations with temperature (ρ = −0.27 and −0.05). full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn this three-year, single-center cohort we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of pediatric viral LRTI in Tianjin, a megacity on the North China Plain, and quantified how closely monthly viral activity tracks ambient weather. To our knowledge, the dataset is unusual for northern China in spanning six respiratory viruses, including the comparatively under-surveyed HRV, HBoV and HMPV, over the full 2023–2025 post-pandemic rebound window, with a complete and time-matched monthly meteorological record.4.1Principal epidemiological featuresAcross the six viruses, HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading causes of pediatric LRTI, and each pathogen carried a well-defined demographic profile. Age and sex stratification confirmed recognized biological gradients. RSV and HBoV were most prevalent in infants and toddlers, in line with airway and immune development (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022); ADV peaked in school-aged children and IFV in the older preschool-to-school-age range, consistent with close-contact transmission in schools and other crowded settings (Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023); and HMPV showed an intermediate distribution. The older age skew of IFV fits its epidemiology in temperate regions, where school-aged children are the principal drivers of seasonal influenza transmission and the group in which symptomatic infection is most readily recognized, in contrast to the infant and toddler predominance of RSV and HBoV (Feng et al., 2024; Klein and Flanagan, 2016). The male predominance for HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV and HMPV, but not IFV, echoes prior pediatric LRTI cohorts and may reflect sex differences in innate immunity and behavior (Klein and Flanagan, 2016). The strong age-group × pathogen association reinforces the need for an explicitly age-stratified surveillance framework.The six pathogens also fell into two distinct seasonal groups. HRV, ADV, RSV, IFV and HMPV all peaked in December, during the cold, dry continental winter, whereas HBoV stood apart with an isolated July maximum—the only warm-season peak of the panel. HRV additionally displayed the broadest seasonal envelope, circulating from March to December, consistent with fundamentally endemic, weakly seasonal behavior. Because the rise in absolute case counts partly reflects expanding testing volume rather than incidence (Section 3.1), the interpretation that follows rests on pathogen composition, age structure and seasonal timing rather than on raw counts.4.2Interpretation in the post-pandemic contextThese patterns are best read against, rather than directly measured against, pre-pandemic Chinese pediatric surveillance, since our cohort describes the post-pandemic period without a matched pre-pandemic Tianjin comparator. Several multi-center Chinese studies contrasting pre-pandemic (2018–2019) with post-pandemic (2023 onward) cohorts have reported a broadly consistent post-pandemic pattern: higher overall pathogen positivity and mixed-infection rates, a higher proportion of severe presentations, and shifts in the relative ranking, seasonal timing and age distribution of individual pathogens (Cui et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). In Shanghai, post-pandemic test positivity rose markedly relative to 2019, with both RSV and ADV increasing and RSV’s onset shifting earlier into August, ahead of its conventional winter season (Liu et al., 2025); other Chinese cohorts spanning the pre-pandemic, pandemic and post-pandemic phases have likewise documented altered seasonal timing and age-distribution shifts for RSV, ADV and rhinovirus after non-pharmaceutical interventions were relaxed (Cui et al., 2024).Interpreted against this backdrop, our Tianjin observations show both continuities and departures. HRV’s endemic, weakly seasonal circulation—reflected in its leading position and broad March–December envelope—appears to have been less perturbed by the pandemic and its aftermath than that of the more strongly seasonal viruses. By contrast, the convergence of five of the six viruses onto a single sharp December peak is consistent with the compressed, intensified post-pandemic winter surge described elsewhere in China, plausibly reflecting the accumulated immunity debt from population-level exposure gaps in 2020–2022 (Cohen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024) superimposed on the resumption of normal contact patterns. HBoV departed most sharply from this winter pattern, peaking instead in summer; to our knowledge, such an isolated warm-season peak has not been prominently reported as a post-pandemic phenomenon elsewhere in China. Whether it reflects a genuine post-pandemic shift in HBoV’s seasonal niche or a feature specific to Tianjin’s continental climate cannot be resolved with a single-center, single-period dataset, and we return to its biological and clinical significance in Section 4.4.4.3Climate-driven lagged effectsThe unadjusted and seasonally adjusted analyses answer different questions, and reading them together guards against a common pitfall in climate–infection studies. In the unadjusted analysis (Table 3), IFV appeared the most climate-responsive virus, with antecedent humidity and temperature aligning with later case counts, in keeping with the recognized seasonal phasing of influenza in temperate climates (Deyle et al., 2016; Kudo et al., 2019; Lowen et al., 2007; Lowen and Steel, 2014). Once seasonality and secular trend were held constant in the unified model, however, these IFV associations disappeared (Table 5). This does not mean that IFV has no climatic drivers. Rather, because ambient temperature and humidity in Tianjin themselves follow an almost perfect annual sinusoid, they are nearly collinear with the sine–cosine seasonal terms of the unified model; for a virus as tightly locked to the annual cycle as influenza (77.5% of deviance explained by season and trend alone), the model simply cannot separate the effect of “season” from that of “temperature” or “humidity.” The most that can be concluded is that, at the present monthly resolution, IFV shows no climatic association detectable independently of the seasonal cycle itself.The seasonally adjusted model instead isolated RSV and HMPV as the only viruses with climate associations independent of shared seasonality (Table 5): RSV tracked temperature and wind speed at short lags, while HMPV tracked temperature positively and humidity inversely, although its low case counts make these estimates imprecise and hypothesis-generating. HRV, ADV and HBoV showed no independent lagged signal, indicating that at monthly resolution their seasonal envelopes are not accompanied by a detectable climate effect beyond the annual cycle. This null result should not be read as evidence of climatic insensitivity. For these three viruses the seasonal-plus-trend baseline itself explained comparatively little of the monthly deviance (HRV 41.5%, HBoV 28.6%, ADV 17.1%; Table 4), so a large share of the variation in their case counts is left unaccounted for by season, trend and weather combined. Residual variation of that magnitude widens the standard errors, and with 36 monthly observations spanning three seasonal cycles only associations of substantial size could reach significance. A modest but real climate effect would probably have escaped detection here, and the finding is better described as uninformative for HRV, ADV and HBoV than as negative. The contrast between the two analyses carries the key methodological lesson: lagged climate associations in surveillance data can be interpreted only after seasonality has been accounted for.These post-pandemic patterns can be read against the pre-pandemic national baseline of Xu et al. (2021), who modelled a seven-virus panel—five of them shared with our own—across 81 sentinel hospitals in 22 Chinese provinces (2009–2013) and ranked the meteorological factors by climate region. For the temperate north, to which Tianjin belongs, three points agree wit…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionAcross 36 months of post-pandemic surveillance in Tianjin (2,597 confirmed cases), HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading viral causes of pediatric LRTI, and each of the six viruses carried a distinctive age, sex, seasonal and specimen-type profile. In a unified model adjusting simultaneously for seasonality and secular trend, RSV and HMPV, rather than IFV, showed the clearest evidence of an independent, non-seasonal climate association, whereas IFV’s prominent unadjusted climate signal proved to reflect its strong intrinsic seasonality. HBoV showed a singular July epidemic at odds with the December convergence of the other viruses, together providing a preliminary basis for pathogen-tailored early warning and prevention in northern Chinese megacities. Co-infection occurred in 4.5% of positives, centered on HRV-containing combinations whose clinical severity remains to be defined. Set alongside pre-pandemic Chinese pediatric surveillance, these findings are broadly consistent with a post-pandemic pattern of intensified, temporally compressed winter transmission, while HBoV’s summer epidemic appears to be a locally distinctive feature warranting further study. If confirmed with higher-resolution, denominator-based data, these findings could inform a hospital-level operational calendar anchored on the December peak and the secondary July HBoV peak, climate-informed early warning tailored to each pathogen’s actual (seasonally adjusted) climate sensitivity, and a refined strategy for vaccination, RSV passive immunization and infection control. Such confirmation will require multi-center cohorts, denominator-based positivity metrics, weekly- or daily-resolution meteorology, and direct pre- versus post-pandemic comparison.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionLower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs)—comprising pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and related lower-airway syndromes—remain leading causes of pediatric hospitalization and mortality in children under five worldwide, with viruses accounting for the overwhelming majority of cases (Nair et al., 2010; Mulholland, 2003; Li et al., 2022). In contrast to generally self-limiting upper respiratory infections, viral LRTIs account disproportionately for admissions requiring supplemental oxygen and intensive care; moreover, certain pathogens, notably RSV and HRV, are implicated in long-term sequelae including recurrent wheeze and asthma (Li et al., 2022; Bizot et al., 2021; Royston and Tapparel, 2016). In China, the burden is amplified by dense urban populations, overlapping pathogen circulation, and the high contact rates among school-aged children, all of which sustain substantial LRTI-related hospitalizations (Cui et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Following the lifting of pandemic-era non-pharmaceutical interventions, several Chinese regions reported atypical, out-of-season resurgences of RSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and ADV (Del Riccio et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). These have been attributed both to an immunity gap accumulated during 2020–2022 and to the re-establishment of pre-pandemic transmission networks (Cohen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Despite this evolving landscape, most national surveillance efforts remain narrowly focused on classical pathogens (RSV, ADV, IFV) or aggregate all respiratory infections irrespective of anatomical site. Consequently, the post-pandemic, multi-pathogen epidemiology of viral LRTI specifically in children—particularly at the city level, where targeted surveillance is most actionable—remains inadequately characterized (Terliesner et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2026).Ambient weather conditions are well-established modulators of respiratory virus transmission, operating through both physical and host-defense mechanisms (Baker et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021). Cold, dry air favors the persistence and airborne dispersal of enveloped viruses such as RSV and influenza by stabilizing the lipid envelope, slowing droplet evaporation, and impairing upper-airway mucociliary clearance (Kudo et al., 2019; Lowen et al., 2007; Lowen and Steel, 2014). Non-enveloped viruses, including ADV and HBoV, whose protein capsids tolerate a wider range of environmental stressors, tend to circulate more evenly throughout the year (Chen et al., 2014b; Lion, 2014). Importantly, climate–virus relationships are non-linear and time-delayed; exposures occurring days to weeks before case surges often exert the dominant effect, a structure that makes distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) particularly suitable for fine-grained inference (Bhaskaran et al., 2013; Gasparrini et al., 2010; Gasparrini, 2011). A recent post-pandemic study from Wuhan, in central China, applied daily-resolution DLNMs to seven respiratory pathogens and identified distinct lagged climate patterns—most notably, humidity drops as 1–2-week antecedents of RSV surges and wind speed as a leading correlate of influenza activity (Li et al., 2025). Because only monthly-resolution meteorological data were available for the present 2023–2025 window (Section 2.3), a full DLNM cross-basis was not identifiable with the available degrees of freedom; we therefore adapted the same distributed-lag logic into a screening framework of single-lag quasi-Poisson models spanning 0–6-month lags, cross-validated against cross-correlation functions and, in a second step, adjusted for seasonality and secular trend within a unified model (Section 2.4). This approach is best viewed as a monthly-resolution approximation to the DLNM framework rather than a full non-linear cross-basis estimation.However, few studies have systematically examined this multi-pathogen landscape in northern China, where the continental monsoon climate—characterized by cold, dry winters; hot, humid summers; and pronounced seasonal swings in temperature, humidity, and wind—differs markedly from the subtropical conditions of Wuhan and other southern cities (Chen et al., 2014a; Cui et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2023). Tianjin, a megacity of 13 million on the North China Plain, offers a particularly valuable setting to address this gap. Its local viral spectrum extends beyond the four classical agents to include three pathogens that are less consistently surveilled but contribute substantially to pediatric LRTI: HRV, HBoV, and HMPV (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020). Prior work in this area has concentrated largely on southern China or on the classical pathogens (RSV, ADV, IFV), and the lagged climatic effects of the less consistently surveilled HRV, HBoV and HMPV under a temperate continental climate have not been systematically evaluated. Our objectives were: (i) to describe the demographic, temporal, and specimen-type distributions of each pathogen; (ii) to characterize co-infection patterns; (iii) to test pathogen-specific associations with monthly meteorological variables using Spearman correlation and season-stratified analyses; and (iv) to evaluate lagged climate effects across 0- to 6-month intervals using cross-correlation functions and a unified quasi-Poisson generalized linear model that simultaneously adjusts for seasonality and secular trends. full_text_excerpt: BackgroundFollowing the lifting of pandemic-era restrictions, China experienced a sharp resurgence in pediatric respiratory infections; however, post-pandemic epidemiological and climatic data on lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from the temperate continental climate of northern China remain scarce.MethodsIn this retrospective, single-center surveillance study, we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of six respiratory viruses in children hospitalized with LRTI in Tianjin and assessed their pathogen-specific, lagged climatic associations. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting and populationWe conducted a retrospective single-center surveillance study at the Department of Respiratory Medicine, Tianjin Children’s Hospital (Ma-Chang campus), the only tertiary-A comprehensive children’s hospital in Tianjin. This last criterion operated at the level of the child rather than of the laboratory result: whenever the tNGS report carried a Class A detection of a bacterial, atypical or non-panel viral pathogen alongside one of the six target viruses, the case was removed from the cohort at eligibility screening, so no such child contributes to any analysis reported here. Children aged 0–18 years hospitalized between January 2023 and December 2025 were tested by targeted next-generation sequencing for human rhinovirus (HRV), adenovirus (ADV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human bocavirus (HBoV), influenza virus (IFV), and human metapneumovirus (HMPV). full_text: AbstractEmerging and re-emerging infectious diseases continue to pose a persistent challenge to global public health security. As an unbiased and noninvasive population-level surveillance approach, wastewater-based epidemiology has emerged as an urban-scale monitoring tool for proactively capturing the community disease burden. In this study, metagenomic and targeted next-generation sequencing were employed to preliminarily characterize wastewater viral communities in Gansu Province from 2024 to 2026. Across the three annual sampling groups, the Simpson diversity index calculated from metagenomic taxonomic profiles showed a significant negative correlation with sampling year. Despite viral enrichment, more than 97% of sequencing reads were assigned to bacteria, likely reflecting residual nonviral nucleic acids and limitations in metagenomic classification. The wastewater virome exhibited a complex host-association spectrum, within which bacteriophages and plant-associated viruses displayed relatively stable community structures and high relative abundances. Among human pathogens, astroviruses were consistently detected at high relative abundances across all samples. Human astrovirus 1 accounted for the largest proportion, and a nearly complete genome sequence of the extraintestinal infection-associated astrovirus MLB2 was recovered. Targeted sequencing further revealed a highly structured environmental enterovirus profile dominated by the species Enterovirus betacoxsackie, followed by Enterovirus alphacoxsackie, whereas Enterovirus coxsackiepol was detected at an extremely low abundance and Enterovirus deconjuncti was not detected. In addition to several common viruses associated with hand, foot, and mouth disease, rare viruses, including coxsackievirus A19 and enterovirus B83, were successfully captured. Echovirus 11 was identified as the predominant enterovirus serotype in current wastewater surveillance in Gansu Province. In summary, this study provides a preliminary characterization of the viral community profiles in wastewater samples from Gansu Province, demonstrates the effectiveness of wastewater-based epidemiology for population-level surveillance, and underscores the need to establish a coordinated defense network integrating clinical case surveillance with environmental monitoring.Keywords: astroviruses, enterovirus, Gansu Province, metagenomic sequencing, targeted next-generation sequencing, wastewater Materials and methodsCollection and processing of the wastewater samplesBetween 2024 and 2026, 18 raw wastewater samples were collected from wastewater treatment plants across 6 cities in Gansu Province (Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Dingxi). Based on their respective sampling years, the samples were categorized into 3 groups: GS24, GS25, and GS26. Seasonal patterns, population differences, and other demographic factors were not considered when defining these groups. Specifically, the sample groups were designated as follows: GS24-1 to GS24-6 were collected in July 2024 from Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Hezuo, respectively; GS25-1 to GS25-6 were collected in June 2025 from Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Zhangye, respectively; and GS26-1 to GS26-6 were collected in March 2026 from Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Dingxi, respectively. GS24-1 and GS24-6 were independently collected on the same day from the same wastewater treatment plant in Hezuo. The same applied to GS25-2 and GS25-6 in Zhangye. The collection dates reflected operational availability and were not selected to provide seasonally matched observations. At each monitoring site, 1 L of raw wastewater was collected. The samples were transported at 4 °C to the laboratory of Gansu Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention within 7 days and processed immediately upon arrival (Wang et al., 2014). For viral concentration, the wastewater samples were initially centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 30 min at 4 °C. Subsequently, 2.5 M MgCl2 was added to the supernatant to achieve a final concentration of 0.05 M, and the pH was adjusted to 3.5 using 0.5 N HCl. The prepared solution was then filtered through a 142-mm cellulose nitrate membrane using a positive-pressure pump. Following filtration, the membrane was fragmented and eluted twice with 10 mL of 3% beef extract by vortexing on ice for 5 min each time. The pooled eluates were centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C and finally passed through a 0.22 μm syringe filter.Nucleic acid extraction and sequencingTotal nucleic acid extraction was performed using the High Pure Viral Nucleic Acid Kit (Roche) without DNase digestion. To reduce potential false-positive results associated with the increased PCR cycles required for capture-based sequencing, the initial extract was divided for parallel and independent library preparations. Metagenomic libraries were generated with the MGIEasy Fast RNA Library Prep Set, whereas the IGT® Fast Stranded RNA Library Prep Kit v2.0 was applied for capture-based construction. For targeted enrichment, a custom enterovirus probe panel was deployed; this panel was specifically designed for selected viruses, encompassing the species Enterovirus alphacoxsackie, Enterovirus betacoxsackie, Enterovirus coxsackiepol, and Enterovirus deconjuncti. Negative controls were processed in parallel during nucleic acid extraction and library preparation to monitor potential contamination, and no evidence of contamination or other procedural abnormalities was observed. Finally, paired-end reads were generated by sequencing the prepared libraries on a DNBSEQ-T7 platform.Sequence data analysisRaw sequencing reads generated by the metagenomic and targeted-capture workflows were assessed using FastQC1 before downstream analysis. No sequencing dataset was excluded from downstream analysis solely on the basis of the FastQC assessment. For raw paired-end reads, adapter trimming and quality filtering (length <50 bp, quality score <20, or containing N bases) were performed using KneadData.2 High-quality reads were then aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) via Bowtie2 to discard host sequences, with the unmapped reads kept for subsequent analyses (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012). Metagenomic reads were taxonomically classified using Kraken2 across multiple taxonomic levels (Wood et al., 2019). All sequencing reads were assembled using MEGAHIT (Li et al., 2015). Contigs (length ≥300 bp, coverage ≥3×) were filtered via awk and annotated using blastn, taking the highest bitscore as the final assignment (Chen et al., 2015). Read abundances per viral species were quantified using BWA-backtrack for downstream evaluation (Li and Durbin, 2009). All astrovirus- and enterovirus-associated contigs assembled using MEGAHIT were extracted from each sample and individually re-evaluated using NCBI BLASTn.3Rarefaction analysis and diversity visualizationAll statistical analyses and data visualizations were performed using R 4.4.3 software.4 Specifically, alpha diversity was assessed at the genus level, and the Shannon and inverse Simpson indices were calculated using the vegan package. Hereafter, the term “Simpson index” refers specifically to the inverse Simpson formulation (1/D). Temporal trends in alpha diversity were assessed using one-tailed Spearman’s rank correlation tests, with the a priori hypothesis that diversity indices would decline over sampling years. Spearman’s rho (ρ) values and corresponding one-sided p values were calculated to evaluate the monotonic relationship between sampling year and alpha diversity indices. Rarefaction curves, heatmaps, stacked bar plots, and visualizations of alpha diversity indices were generated using the ggplot2 package.Quantitative profiling of the viromeFor the quantitative analysis of viral communities, relative abundances were estimated using the reads per million normalization method described in Equation 1. The mapped read counts of each viral contig were adjusted for genome length differences by dividing the read counts by the average genome size of the corresponding viral family or genus. Subsequently, the adjusted read counts were normalized against the total number of reads assigned to all viral families or genera within each individual sample (Worp et al., 2025). This normalization strategy was consistently applied to all heatmaps generated in this study.However, a modified approach was applied for the stacked bar charts illustrating the relative abundances of different species within the genus Enterovirus. Because genome lengths among enterovirus serotypes are highly conserved, with an average size of approximately 7.4 kb, genome length normalization was omitted when calculating the relative abundance of enterovirus-associated contigs.(1)Relative abundance=virus readsaverage genome length×total viral reads×106The host type classifications for the viral families listed herein were retrieved from the Virus-Host Database.5Comparison of viral diversityTo compare viral community structure across sample groups, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on centered log-ratio transformed abundance data (Gloor et al., 2017). Zero counts in the abundance matrices were replaced with a pseudocount equivalent to half of the minimum positive abundance value detected within the respective dataset, as centered log-ratio transformation requires strictly positive values. Viral taxa contributing most strongly to the principal components were identified based on the magnitude of their loadings. PCA biplots were generated using the ggplot2 package in R 4.4.3 software, with 68% confidence ellipses overlaid to visualize group clustering.Phylogenetic analysisReference viral VP1 gene sequences were retrieved from GenBank at the National Center for biotechnology information (NCBI). These sequences, together with the VP1 sequences generated in this study, were aligned using MAFFT v7.520 (Katoh and Standley, 2013). Neighbor-joining (NJ) phylogenetic trees were constructed in MEGA7 based on evolutionary distances calculated using the maximum composite likelihood method (Kumar et al., 2016). The robustness of the inferred tree topologies was assessed by bootstrap analysis with 1,000 replicates (Felsenstein, 1985), and bootstrap support values of 70% or higher were displayed at the corresponding nodes. Supplementary materialThe Supplementary material for this article can be found online at: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmicb.2026.1966428/full#supplementary-material Supplementary Materials ResultsBetween-year variation in alpha diversity and broad taxonomic compositionRarefaction analysis showed that the sequencing captured most of the detectable genus-level diversity across the three sampling groups, indicating that the sequencing depth was sufficient (Figure 1A). Overall metagenomic sequencing statistics and alpha diversity indices (including the Shannon and Simpson indices) are summarized in Table 1 and visualized in Figures 1B,C. Sampling year was treated as an ordinal variable. The Shannon index showed a negative but nonsignificant correlation with sampling year (Spearman’s ρ = −0.354, p = 0.075). In contrast, the Simpson index exhibited a significant negative correlation with sampling year (Spearman’s ρ = −0.472, p = 0.024). Given that the dataset comprised only three annual sampling campaigns conducted in different months, these analyses were considered exploratory assessments of between-year variation. At the broadest taxonomic level, more than 97% of reads in each dataset were assigned to Bacteria, whereas no more than 0.94% were classified as viral (Table 2). Following taxonomic classification with Kraken2, 56.42–74.74% of the metagenomic reads across samples remained unclassified at the genus level (Supplementary Table S1). In this context, “unclassified” indicates that the reference database and parameter settings did not provide sufficient evidence for a reliable taxonomic assignment. The unclassified reads were not subjected to further characterization in this study.Figure 1Overview of metagenomic sequencing data across the three groups. (A) Rarefaction curves at the genus level.
